en: In the month of Mārkaḻi, on this good day when the moon is full,
you who would go to bathe, come! Come, you with fine jewels!
Rich young girls of Āyppāṭi, brimming with wealth!
The son of Nandagopa, fierce in deed with his sharp spear,
the young lion of Yaśodā of the lovely eyes,
dark-bodied, red-eyed, with a face like the radiant moon,
Nārāyaṇa himself will give us the paṟai,
so that the people of the earth may praise us, plunge in and bathe! Ēlōr empāvāy!
notes: Romanized as written, including the metrical splits of the printed text ('nantakō paṉkumaraṉ' for Nantakōpaṉ kumaraṉ, 'nārā yaṇaṉē' for Nārāyaṇaṉē) and the stray space before the comma in line 2 ('pōtumiṉō ,nēriḻaiyīr'). ISO 15919 for Tamil: letters as written (k, c, ṭ, t, p whatever their sound), ṉ ன, ṟ ற, ḻ ழ, ḷ ள, e/ē and o/ō kept apart.

line 6: kathir-mathiyam is read two ways: 'the radiant (full) moon' (as the Wikisource gloss has it, மதியம் = full moon) or 'the sun (katir) and the moon (matiyam)', a face both bright and cool. I chose the first; note the second.
line 7: paṟai is a drum, here also the boon the girls ask for at the end of their vow (the drum they will play, and what they are 'given'). Kept untranslated.

line 8: 'ēlōr empāvāy' is the refrain of all thirty verses of the pāvai vow. ēl and ōr are usually taken as particles of exhortation or as meaningless refrain syllables; em pāvāy is 'our maiden / our pāvai' (the image of the goddess made for the vow, or the girls addressing one another). Kept as a refrain, not translated.
line 1: Mārkaḻi, the Tamil month of December-January; 'mati niṟainta', 'the moon full'.
line 3: Āyppāṭi, 'the herdsmen's village' (Gokula), kept as a name.
line 4: koṭun-toḻilaṉ, 'he of cruel / fierce work' (Nandagopa guarding the herds against enemies of the child Krishna).
